expansion:
This presentation is anterior uveitis: the lecture lists ocular pain, red eye, photophobia, and blurred vision, with ciliary injection and anterior-chamber “Cells & flare” as clinical features (L13,14, slide 13, 14, 16). A topical cycloplegic-mydriatic agent is therefore the essential addition to topical corticosteroids. The lecture states that these medications decrease “photophobia and pain from iritis and ciliary spasm” and “prevent and break recently formed posterior synechiae” (L13,14, slide 20). Posterior synechiae are also specifically listed as a sequela of anterior uveitis (L13,14, slide 18).

Topical pilocarpine is wrong because it is a miotic, so it constricts rather than cyclopleges and dilates the pupil; it would not achieve the stated pain relief or prevention of posterior synechiae (not taken from the course material). The lecture lists pilocarpine among topical miotics for glaucoma, not anterior uveitis (not taken from the course material).

A topical beta-blocker is wrong because it lowers intraocular pressure rather than relieving ciliary spasm or maintaining pupillary dilation (not taken from the course material). The uveitis lecture reserves antiglaucoma medication for “case of increased IOP” (L13,14, slide 20), whereas this question asks for the routine adjunct that addresses pain and synechiae.

Oral NSAIDs are wrong because they do not provide cycloplegia or mydriasis and therefore cannot prevent posterior synechiae (not taken from the course material). In this lecture, oral NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are identified as the main treatment for episcleritis (L13,14, slide 31) and are also listed for scleritis (L13,14, slide 37), not as the required adjunct in anterior uveitis.
objective: In anterior uveitis, topical cycloplegic-mydriatic medication relieves ciliary-spasm pain and prevents or breaks recently formed posterior synechiae.
